title: Sidekick or star of the show?
caption: A field of stars and galaxies beside the cluster NGC 299, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hundreds of distant stars and galaxies fill this Hubble frame, yet the object Hubble was actually studying is nowhere to be seen. The Advanced Camera for Surveys has two detectors. One recorded the real target, an open star cluster called NGC 299, while the other photographed the patch of sky just next to it. This is that second view.

It is technically a sidekick picture, but it is full of interest. Many of the tiny objects that look like stars are really galaxies. The spirals show arms curving out from bright centers, while fuzzier, less defined shapes may be elliptical galaxies. Some hold millions upon millions of stars, yet are so far away that all of them fit into a pinprick no bigger than a single star.

Blue points mark very hot stars, a few stretched into crosses by the struts that hold Hubble's secondary mirror. Red points mark cooler stars, perhaps red giants, dying stars that have cooled and swollen.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this field through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so part of this picture records light we could never see directly.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The Advanced Camera for Surveys is a highly efficient wide-field camera that covers both visible and near-infrared light.
alt: A field of bright blue and redder stars, some with cross-shaped spikes, among many small spiral and fuzzy galaxies.
